implementation_notes: Ruby's dup and clone are shallow, so the memento that actually protects history is a Marshal round-trip: Marshal.dump writes the object graph (or whatever marshal_dump returns) and Marshal.load reconstitutes a detached copy, with the freeze: true argument deep-freezing the restored snapshot so a careless caretaker cannot mutate it. Implement marshal_dump/marshal_load on the originator to decide exactly what a snapshot contains - which also keeps non-dumpable collaborators out of it - and let an Array or a capped stack play the caretaker. The shallow variants (dup, clone, Struct copies) are sound only when every captured value is immutable, which in Ruby means frozen.
pitfalls: Marshal.load on untrusted data is a remote-code-execution vector - the documentation is explicit that it must never receive user-supplied input, so history must come from your own process or trusted storage.
Some objects cannot be dumped at all (IO instances, Procs, Method objects, Threads, singleton objects, anonymous classes); they raise TypeError unless marshal_dump deliberately excludes them.
Marshalling copies the whole graph, so snapshotting a large document per keystroke is expensive; use it at checkpoints or pair it with an immutable-state fast path.
A dumped snapshot is bound to the class and to the marshal format version, so renaming the class or upgrading Ruby versions needs a migration path for stored history.

variants.name: Frozen immutable state + dup snapshots
variants.idiom_name: Struct of frozen values, dup'ed into the history
variants.implementation_notes: If every captured value is immutable (frozen strings, symbols, numbers, frozen literals), a shallow copy is a sound memento because nothing can mutate the shared values afterwards: Object#dup returns an unfrozen copy of the container, Object#clone preserves the frozen state and singleton class, and freezing the state on write makes sharing safe. This is the cheapest realization - no marshalling, no I/O - and the one Ruby's freeze discipline nudges you toward; it breaks the moment a captured value is a mutable Array or Hash, so the originator must freeze deeply or restrict the state to frozen scalars.
pitfalls: dup copies the container, not its contents: a Struct whose members are mutable strings or arrays shares them with the live object, so every captured value must be frozen.
freeze is shallow as well - freezing a Hash does not freeze its keys and values, so nested data needs recursive freezing.
clone preserves frozen state and the singleton class while dup returns an unfrozen copy; picking the wrong one either raises FrozenError on the next write or leaves a snapshot mutable.
